Examples would include man against man, man against nature, issues involving what is right or wrong, etc., Resolution of conflict Theme, i.e. the central or underlying meaning or dominant idea(s) that structures a narrative. It should be noted, however, that theme is not a textual structure that every reader interprets in exactly the same way. Characterization- Main character in a story; Stock and/or flat characters, i.e. characters with only one or two qualities or traits. Stereotypes, such as the mean stepmother, are examples of flat characters., Archetypes, e.g. the hero/heroine archetype, the villain, forces of good and evil such as superheroes (Reading only); Setting-  The physical landscap and social context in which the action of story occurs, i.e. its time and place and  Descriptive details that construct the world of the story (e.g. the forest in Max’s room allows the reader to move into the story); Other features of narrative- Literary conventions (e.g. "Once upon a time" in a fairy tale, moral in a fable), Humor, suspense, repetition and Dialogue, e.g. to reveal character, Point of view, i.e. narrative voice in first or third person

Plot structure and features Use of images (photos or drawings) to extend the story and to provide story details, Use of music and/or sound to create suspense, mood, humor, conflict, etc. (Viewing only); Use of colour to suggest emotion, to create mood, etc. Use of different scenes or episodes to move the story forward (Viewing only); C haracterization Surface appearance of a character (e.g. clothing, physical attributes), Use of details to convey an imaginary character (e.g. wings, exaggerated or invented facial features), Use of explanation marks and speech bubbles to show thought and dialogue, e.g. in comic books or some animation films, Use of body language and gesture to convey character traits, including emotions (Viewing only), Use of music and/or sound to signal or stress some aspect of character, e.g. music to signal the reappearance of a character such as Tinkerbell or Captain Hook in Peter Pan (Viewing only), Use of camera angle (e.g. use of low angle to make someone look stronger or like a bully, high angle to make someone look weaker or vulnerable), Stereotypes of individuals and groups (e.g. perceptions about gender in comics and picture books) (Viewing only); Setting Repetition of symbols, or motifs, to create mood, suspense, sense of continuity (e.g. scenes of the ocean in a story that takes place in Cape Breton) (Viewing only), Use of light and dark (e.g. to create a sense of foreboding, to change time frame) (Viewing only), Clothing and other details that create a sense of time and location

66A5058EDA424A57A5381E4FE1EFE6B8.description: Spoken and Written Texts: Plot structures and features- Predictable story patterns, Sequence of events, Incidents (e.g. actions that take place in the story usually related to the main conflict); Foreshadowing, i.e. the use of hints or clues to suggest what will happen later in the story (Reading only), Flashback (Reading only), Episodes, e.g. typically the subject of a chapter (Reading only), Conflict, i.e. central problem around which a story is typically organized. Examples would include man against man, man against nature, issues involving what is right or wrong, etc., Resolution of conflict Theme, i.e. the central or underlying meaning or dominant idea(s) that structures a narrative. It should be noted, however, that theme is not a textual structure that every reader interprets in exactly the same way. Characterization- Main character in a story; Setting-  The physical landscap and social context in which the action of story occurs, i.e. its time and place and  Descriptive details that construct the world of the story (e.g. the forest in Max’s room allows the reader to move into the story); Other features of narrative- Literary conventions (e.g. "Once upon a time" in a fairy tale, moral in a fable), Humor, suspense, repetition and Dialogue, e.g. to reveal character, Point of view, i.e. narrative voice in first or third person, Attitude of author to the material, i.e. writer’s position (Reading only)

0EFD2EC2D98F4F14BFC6BAB8EB2D308C.description: Structures, Features, Codes and Conventions of Argumentative Texts The student understands the purpose of the following and uses this knowledge to construct meaning when reading and producing spoken, written, media, multigenre and multimodal texts:

B5351B5146D948769AD64D543715B7BF.description: Required Argumentative Texts The student reads and produces the following texts:

62973D8710D84406AFD6829EB4F7484B.description: Exposition: Argumentative Texts. Argumentative texts try to convince people of a point of view about a topic or issue through a logical sequencing of ideas and/or propositions.

87E65F0B4A034675BDBE87DA7A7F4AFF.description: Reviews: Introduction that includes: the title and name of producer of the text being reviewed; an overview of the main topic, genre, critiques and issues raised, Content which includes: background on author and context; comparison with other texts in same genre; critique of producer’s decisions (e.g. particular aspects of the plot, characters, setting, conflicts, theme(s), and/or various literary techniques),Organizational structure that supports the reviewer’s opinion/critique (e.g. compare/contrast, respecting narrative chronology), Conclusion which contains a positive, negative or ambivalent recommendation and Conventions to establish credibility (e.g. informal but expert tone and diction, 1st person point of view)

887A77840A224B6392467743620AE9E1.description: Advertisements (including PSAs): Persuasive techniques such as appeals to basic needs (e.g. ‘fitting in’,‘luxury and style’, ‘doing good’; emotional appeals such as use of testimonials and sad music) and Media conventions such as camera language, layout, colour, sound (jingle, repetition, rhyme, voiceover).

767A593A7F0A4F49BAA5F84A01E2A9E0.description: Respect for production constraints that influence the content of a newspaper/magazine/show (e.g. word limit, time restrictions, readership tastes and expectations, layout)

26B4DE8606D44A1BAF58304219F17FEB.description: Persuasive language such as connotation, loaded words, modals (should, would, must), polarizing rhetoric, judging/quantifying/qualifying words

CED9626ED8904F2A8EEB3A1208D630F7.description: Figurative language (e.g. imagery, metaphor, simile, personification)

9FEF94404051472EA9CC56046FD185BA.description: Figures of speech (e.g. metonymy, euphemism, oxymoron, hyperbole and understatement)

470C602238614DC8BA6FABC2F9C9D48A.description: Humour (e.g. bathos, double-entendre, pun, parody, sarcasm)

3D1908CCD4F64ECCB9CAB9E425DC92EB.description: Structures, Features, Codes and Conventions of Persuasive Texts The student understands the purpose of the following and uses this knowledge to construct meaning when reading and producing spoken, written, media, multigenre and multimodal texts:

5C9EC5BC9C4045179A7E16C0BADC8E86.description: Advertisements, including public service announcements (PSAs), posters, book trailer

D437B147974D4779A580F344EC7C7538.description: Speeches (e.g. pitch an ad campaign, book talk)

866F2C36BCF346159DF12C620DCAD118.description: Texts dealing with personal and social concerns (i.e. Internet sites, documentary films, speeches)

6EBC2EDDD57E44918ED8429F2C56FD2E.description: Reviews (e.g. of books, television programs, films, music)

8DDAA71A2EA5494B99E99CC29C2D15A6.description: Advertisements, including public service announcements (PSAs), publicity campaigns, popular slogans, posters, book and film trailers.

4CDE8B47ECCB42F08AFDCE5470C9A1CC.description: Required Persuasive Texts The student reads and produces the following texts

5D5A6EE45ED3420BA6BEE0474D220C3B.description: Exposition: Persuasive Texts Persuasive texts try to move people to act or behave in a certain way, including selling or promoting a product or ideology

10D43980C5C74545ACB3FDA85E9A9ACC.description: Expository Texts Expository texts are constructed in deliberate ways and interpret some aspect of the world in a particular way. Whereas fictional texts may occupy a prominent place in our leisure time, persuasive and argumentative texts are central not only to leisure activities, as in reading newspapers, but also play an important role in postsecondary institutions, different professions and in the world of work in general.

C7144CC09F8E4F07A85CADF41CA7ABF4.description: Interviews:Question and answer (Q & A) structure, including short biographical introduction, open-ended and relevant questions, and follow-up questions: Rhetorical strategies to construct a relationship with the subject such as sharing short anecdotes, contextualizing, eye contact, paraphrasing, showing knowledge of subjec

E0EBA14E2F3241C6ACBB30C199A31B2B.description: Research reports : Structure that matches the information reported and expectations of a specific discipline/field of study (e.g. science, social studies):Cause/effect and chronolog and Classification and compare/contras:Visual conventions to convey information, meaning(s) and relationships among ideas such as in a timeline or mind map (e.g. key words and images, colour, lines, arrows, dimension and spacing): Features that elucidate/develop the content: paraphrasing, using examples, description, quotations, definitions Conventions that establish authority and expertise(e.g. formal register, technical/disciplinary diction/word choice, passive voice, proper referencing of sources)

892BC95C388041C78DDF87A8DAFE0723.description: News reports :Inverted pyramid structure in short breaking news story (i.e. answering W5 in descending order ofimportance):Features that give a sense of immediacy and prescience in a breaking news report: active voice, simple syntax and diction, eye-witness quotations and photo w/caption: Structure that suits the subject of a feature story (e.g. chronology in a profile/human interest story; cause/effect in an issues-based feature; parallel/convergent structure to interconnect two or more stories with the same theme): Features that give a sense of depth and context in a feature news story: background information, flashback, anecdotes, interview data, research information from both sides of the issue: Respect for the production constraints that influence content (e.g. word limit, time restrictions, copyright, ideology):Media conventions for specific effect (e.g. using camera angle and graphics to convey credibility; using on-site correspondent and hand held camera to create a sense of embeddedness)

365B00CCE6A24F62928100C41A831ABC.description: Conclusion(s) which highlight important facts or findings (e.g. via synthesis, interpretation of data, recommendations

BF6D388F5DF64389B1B61B0B3BF3F5DB.description: Evidence to support details, ideas, concepts (e.g. via a variety of primary sources such as field notes, interviews, artefacts; and, secondary sources such as facts, statistics, contextual information

77E7C805259249878737401DAD19A88C.description: Information organized and sequenced using a structure such as chronology, classification, compare/contrast, problem/solution, cause/effect

222C9CC030D4444FA70D006326421AC8.description: Conventions which indicate cause and effect (e.g. clear and precise diction/word choice; causal conjunctions such as because, consequently and therefore; temporal conjunctions such as first, second, when and then; transitional phrases such as for example, in other words, as a result) d.   Visuals to focus reader’s attention on what is most

5824815230004FDC9AB8ACE3A6F3D7F4.description: Selection and synthesis of steps in a process

D2354F44779D424DB20C1821AAB5E559.description: Explanations of a process (e.g. teaching something to peers/class, sharing expertise with others)

04CBA70BE8A948C68BF6271D2989B383.description: Explanations of a process (e.g. presentation of a lesson by teacher and/or peers)

F42275FCEB4F49FB8DADCCEC83F692DA.description: Conventions of specific literary genres (e.g. use of mythical characters in an allegory; scene gathering all the suspects in a mystery; quest plot structure in a fantasy; plot twist in a tragedy)

938B0FFC3959488483B409BC327C5E6A.description: Editorials:Focus on current issues and events in the news,Introduction which situates issue within a local and/or national context,  Stance/role of editor is consistent with the ideology of a given news source and Respect for production constraints that influence the editorial content of a newspaper/magazine/show (e.g. the influence of producer’s political ideology on content; word limit, time restrictions, copyright)

731E25F15F904B5DA301B5A51F3D4151.description: Essays: Introduction which includes a lead, an elaboration of the topic, a clear thesis statement and a path statement, Evidence organized as points in a logical sequence (e.g. using a structure such as classification, cause and effect, compare/contrast,chronology), Conventions to establish a sense of unity and coherence (i.e. paragraphs structured using a formulaic pattern: topic sentence, explanation of the example/idea, evidence to support that example/idea, and reasoning to link back to thesis),Conclusion which wraps up the argument by: generalizing the thesis/ideas to the human condition, elevating specific issues to a universal level, drawing on higher truths, etc. and Proper citation(s) of reference material (e.g. ellipsis points, brackets, formatting, footnotes, bibliography )

2D3C0F93436F4B93AF91519C252BAFEA.description: Debates:Use of a procedure such as Parliamentary procedure,Basic structure: opening statement of the issue and a preview of main arguments, followed by arguments for a point of view with supporting evidence, then arguments against this point of view, time for rebuttal, and concluding with a recommendation in favour of one side ,Rhetorical strategies to address and/or distract opponent such as rephrasing, paraphrasing, and/or redirecting to move debate forward; maintaining eye-contact; using a rational, unwavering tone; and fallacies such as red herring, ad hominem argument, guilt by association/bad company, straw man, Spoken conventions such as intonation patterns, pauses and silences, gestures, turn-taking, use of a moderator and (Reading only) Media conventions for specific effect (e.g. the use of close-up to create a sense of immediacy or involvement in a televised debate)

C8E9C4DA5BF0465C976E3FE37F4A344E.description: Multimodal conventions (e.g. video clips of recent news events in a panel discussion; satirical cartoon with an editorial on same topic)

AFFA4A65B662495EB84F9609ED58FDEB.description: Multigenre conventions (e.g. use of personal narrative in an essay; ‘call to action’ conclusion in an editorial)

2DEED33AFEED4F948DD075D565FC0D46.description: Conventions which establish relationships between ideas and serve to extend the argument (e.g. syntactic structures such as parallel structure and syllogism;transitional words and phrases such as however, subsequently, on the other hand; correlative conjunctions such as if, … then …, rather … than

DB9785A7FE6342B4B4ACFBE9B433D9F2.description: Conventions to establish credibility and authority such as using a formal, academic register; 1st or 3rd person point of view; timeless present tense and passive voice; precise, factual, and/or technical language

5A417B35DFFA4550ACA6837F43D5CC8F.description: Rhetorical strategies to engage and convince reader (e.g. stating basis of argument (pros/cons) upfront, anticipating and addressing opposing viewpoints; using analogies; using historical and/or current events to situate topic; deductive/inductive reasoning, antithesis; and fallacies such as burden of proof, false dilemma/black and white thinking, false cause/non sequitur)

6F5C41065E964613AA272C9C42C939BD.description: Structures, Features, Codes and Conventions of Argumentative Texts The student understands the purpose of the following and uses this knowledge to construct meaning when reading and producing spoken, written, media, multigenre and multimodal texts:

FAC5E2C865E8440F9457A17FFBDF703E.description: Essays dealing with issues arising from literature (i.e. literary essay)

55ED1534E2BA454E8A4948653B271BF8.description: Texts dealing with personal and social concerns (e.g. editorial, blog, research thesis)

531DD0ABDC93421DB49EB1F47438385B.description: Essays dealing with issues/topics arising from literature, popular culture and the media

3F2B64BE446D44AD879781F9CB6A00E8.description: Texts dealing with personal and social concerns, such as political blogs, editorials, televised panel discussions, critical essays

75AD1E1CA63C411DB4694859827E8F7A.description: Required Argumentative Texts The student reads and produces the following texts:

4612BFC7D4DF4B2B9BB36173A88F8B18.description: Exposition: Argumentative Texts. Argumentative texts try to convince people of a point of view about a topic or issue through a logical sequencing of ideas and/or propositions.

68D64C59AA4C4A9A8C99FC6223DED1C0.description:
Essays :Thesis/controlling idea (i.e. thesis statement),Introduction with an engaging lead and an elaboration of topic, Evidence organized as points in a logical sequence (i.e. using a structure such as classification, cause and effect, compare/contrast, chronology),Use of a variety of strategies to prove/illustrate point (e.g. anecdote, famous quotations, popular media examples) and Conclusion which convinces reader either to behave (buy, donate, act
– ‘call to action’) or to think a certain way

7155610F706B4DF888D1EC7CFD47F9BB.description: Reviews: Introduction that includes: the title and name of producer of the text being reviewed; an overview of the main topic, genre, critiques and issues raised, Content which includes: background on author and context; comparison with other texts in same genre; critique of producer’s decisions (e.g. particular aspects of the plot, characters, setting, conflicts, theme(s), and/or various literary techniques),Organizational structure that supports the reviewer’s opinion/critique (e.g. compare/contrast, respecting narrative chronology), Conclusion which contains a positive, negative or ambivalent recommendation and Conventions to establish credibility (e.g. informal but expert tone and diction, 1st person point of view)

89FD1E96B08D452DA7FE3E574BCD0847.description: Advertisements (including PSAs): Persuasive techniques such as appeals to basic needs (e.g. ‘fitting in’,‘luxury and style’, ‘doing good’; emotional appeals such as use of testimonials and sad music), Media conventions such as camera language, layout, colour, sound (jingle, repetition, rhyme, voiceover), Manipulation of familiar codes and conventions for specific effect and Transformation of ideas/concept from one mode/medium to another (e.g. creating a spoof PSA based on a current news story)

B5B79BC439DA4186822144B8CEAEDAD6.description: Multimodal conventions (e.g. sound of grasshoppers to indicate deafening silence in a speech; manipulated images in an op-ed piece)

9712C673499B4DBFB2DF8CC5D461897C.description: Multigenre conventions (e.g. use of melodrama in a series of TV ads; use of fairy tale conventions in an opinion column)

2BE97007D06D42738F3F57BFF4EE25EE.description: Respect for production constraints that influence the content of a newspaper/magazine/show (e.g. word limit, time restrictions, readership tastes and expectations, layout)

02684B5058684EAE94C9FD5B9BE00B27.description: Persuasive language such as connotation, loaded words, modals (should, would, must), polarizing rhetoric, judging/quantifying/qualifying words

1B17EE68CDF9490684D8BBB792B6A785.description: Humour (e.g. bathos, double-entendre, pun, parody, sarcasm)

AB726A5A62F9432ABC0BDABF53E59C09.description: Essays dealing with personal and social concerns (e.g. opinion column, position paper)

253C5144F9034EFF846E9F1558EAF5C0.description: Advertisements, including public service announcements (PSAs), posters, book trailer

321FF0FF2637495D96DA150CCDAB4EF9.description: Texts dealing with personal and social concerns (i.e. Internet sites, documentary films, speeches)

85E0119B12AC4116B6DDC7A534888167.description: Reviews (e.g. of books, television programs, films, music)

AE72D3704593487DBB2443B4A000DDA3.description: Applies principles for maintaining his/her balance in various postures (e.g. In a complex posture on hands or feet, one’s base should be widened to maintain balance.)

30F7FCE82C7648AEA577FE15EA9B3DFA.description: Defines some terms that must be understood in reference to justice (e.g. injustice, right, law, fairness, equality, merit, eugenics, euthanasia)

C62CE3465C2D4E53B95FF6DAD8835FDF.description: Makes connections between the future of humanity and the recognition of others

DCA743CCE8334348B665F7580478466D.description: Makes connections between the future of humanity and the pursuit of the common good

A8000E6C7B98403488D3F3894B9C8488.description: Makes connections between ethical reflection on the future of humanity and ethical reflection on tolerance, justice or human ambivalence

94BB86078B2C4EFA80A85AAE6D4155F1.description: Names references that support and enrich ethical reflection on the future of humanity (e.g. charters, laws, regulations, science, individuals, media)

91B281DC273E4C929D52946D7E458399.description: Formulates ethical questions on the future of humanity (e.g. Why should human beings be concerned with the future of humanity?)

98F1B87D847648929429C07C88AE661D.description: Gives examples of how certain references can guide individual or group actions in the face of challenges to the future of humanity (e.g. the value of respect for the environment [reference] inspires certain people to buy local products in order to avoid transportation over long distances)

2CBD954672384E60B0901E0AEA804329.description: Explains some possible actions or options, given the challenges in the relationship between human beings and the environment (e.g. composting or burning organic matter): description of the action, intention, people involved,values, possible consequences, etc.

BFFF9747C4A042D086D954DEBC80E010.description: Explains some current challenges in the relationship between human beings and the environment (e.g. exploitation of natural resources, space exploration, research into genetics and GMOs): issues, actors involved,statistics, scope of the problem tensions, values and norms at stake, etc.

48B267AD22814B558F216636825E48E3.description: Explains some possible actions or options, given the challenges in human relations (e.g. fair trade, economic protectionism): description of the action, intention, people involved,values, possible consequences, etc.

69A995910F784999AB3084C2EA7628EA.description: Explains some current challenges in human relations (e.g. the gap between rich and poor countries, the consequences of overpopulation):. issue, actors involved, statistics, scope of the problem tensions, values and norms at issue, etc,

4A827CC239AA4B768022E73933175790.description: Explains different ways to look at the future of humanity (e.g. Aldous Huxley presents an imaginary vision of the future in a society dominated by science; the reflections of Hubert Reeves and David Suzuki remind us of the importance of protecting the environment to ensure the future of humanity)

1A8EED1BCB9B41C9A71CD3EE9F92EC19.description: Makes connections between tolerance and the recognition of others

9E8AB84E157B42E295CDFDF9E77D4404.description: Makes connections between tolerance and the pursuit of the common good

F9D64B9269A241DB81A312BE7E5C7865.description: Makes connections between ethical reflection on tolerance and ethical reflection on the future of humanity, justice or human ambivalence

4A969EFF693C464D86515682A2D74644.description: Names references that support and enrich ethical reflection on tolerance (e.g. charters, laws, regulations, individuals, media, UNESCO’s Declaration of Principles on Tolerance)

6BD8E8E16E13441B8A350B0846EF6976.description: Formulates ethical questions about tolerance (e.g. What is the difference between complacency and tolerance?)

273161BB8F744A7685F5FBC005391848.description: Explains different individual or collective responses to cases taken from literature or current events that can be sources of tension regarding tolerance: the actions taken, the values involved ,the laws and regulations to be considered, possible consequences, etc

FE308296C72B44A4ACC9C9F235C40ED7.description: Based on cases taken from literature or current affairs, describes examples of tolerance, intolerance or indifference: origin of the situation, people involved, people’s reactions, circumstances, place, issues at stake, etc

C6F6F9CBD65A484FB4CC60F3C75B7100.description: Gives examples of current topics that can be sources of tension regarding tolerance (e.g. same-sex marriage, the integration of handicapped persons, requests from religious groups)

B1956ADE6A4D4FC3A4BEAA5E373CECA2.description: Defines terms that can be associated with tolerance (e.g. intolerance, indifference, discrimination, segregation, racism, xenophobia, reasonable accommodation, diversity)

85572C63B0D7434EAC471C5804488FC6.description: Names references that support and enrich ethical reflection on the social order (e.g. charters, laws, regulations, individuals, media)

0D55752B81C24021930D7DA3526B1F98.description: Formulates ethical questions about the social order (e.g. What behaviour should be encouraged or avoided when faced with a law that is considered unfair?)

F6B18A8C426D45B785F592F5A159F2A0.description: Shows how values can inspire a person or a group to question or uphold the social order and the law (e.g. in the name of justice, a people rises up against the authoritative regime in power; for health reasons, a group of students advocates strict enforcement of the no-smoking legislation)

25C37FA1AF6C408C802EF9C80D5A0B4E.description: Names factors that could bring about a change in social values and norms (e.g. war, immigration, the media, science)

3D520EEF4395448E8C736B0602D2B562.description: Describes different forms of disobedience (e.g. crime [serious, voluntary offence against the law]; civil disobedience [passive resistance and refusal to obey a law that is deemed to be unfair])

DD001ECE0F6743F8924D45FDF36F325C.description: Describes different forms of obedience (e.g. submission [agreeing to submit without protest]; conformity [adopting the same behaviour as the majority])

548CBA2B1348479994B8C593C95A900C.description: Describes different forms of power in groups, institutions or organizations (e.g. authoritative power [imposition of will]; democratic power [taking into account the majority vote by electing representatives])

F5BB4BC1AF6442EA818A55EA877328EC.description: Uses examples to show that the social order is based on the values and norms adopted by groups, institutions and organizations (e.g. in many families, the social order is based on the values of love and sharing, as well as on family rules; in a theatre company, the social order is based on the director’s instructions [norms] as well as on the values of rigour and perseverance)

C724F748E4364BC2B603869336F13265.description: Names references that support and enrich ethical reflection on autonomy (e.g. charters, laws, regulations, individuals, media)

DA4B644180504791A8580DF3CEDF1700.description: Formulates ethical questions about autonomy (e.g. Is it possible to be entirely autonomous? Why or why not?)

081EF30073F64EB79A6710AC747E9A8C.description: Explains how exercising one’s autonomy can become a source of tension (e.g. after deciding to dress in a certain style, an adolescent may come into conflict with his or her parents)

335C7FC3FD0F4E7F99678366EBDC8FB5.description: Shows how friendship, love, academic success, consumption, thrill-seeking, etc., can lead to autonomy or to dependence (e.g. a young person gains self-confidence through friendships with her peers and decides to look for a summer job; a young person enjoys playing music so much that he cannot stop and neglects his responsibilities)

B40EAB1F26A44419B3AB78A590846176.description: Names conditions that foster autonomy (e.g. critical judgment, good sense, moral responsibility, the ability to choose, authenticity, resourcefulness)

20474C3942DD41CD9B5CFA4A8B718F86.description: Gives examples of signs of dependence in individuals or groups (e.g. a person who cannot stop playing online games; modern society cannot function without electricity)

3BD0A19DA50843FB8629B2F0C8A027EE.description: Gives different definitions of the word dependence (e.g. the inability to develop one’s potential without someone else’s help; the state of a person who cannot carry out daily tasks alone)

E3ECF45CABC84897AABDBCAD8D904891.description: Gives examples of signs of autonomy in individuals or groups (e.g. a visually impaired person goes out alone with a guide dog; team members organize their own practice when their coach is absent)

72638CBCFF92433FA4051109B3CFCEF7.description: Gives different definitions of autonomy (e.g. ability to live without anyone’s help; right to self-government)

DF33B1F713D64F48A26E41B186DD2067.description: Names references that support and enrich ethical reflection on freedom (e.g. charters, laws, regulations, individuals, media)

3D2AD856E28D493095EAF77CF3093397.description: Formulates ethical questions about freedom (e.g. How does freedom imply limits?)

2E38C98BB1A34B44836DB1B7B4F43FEA.description: Uses examples to show how responsibilities, rights and duties limit the exercise of freedom (e.g. the freedom to express an opinion in a student newspaper does not relieve the authors of the obligation to avoid damaging another person’s reputation)

1247CBD8EED344D3B509B0B9B25E3A1A.description: Makes connections between the exercise of freedom in private and in public (e.g. one expresses love for one’s sweetheart differently in private and in public; e-mailing a personal photo to a friend does not authorize him/her to publish it on a social network)

1C4C02C7404E443EBEF27D6C568D4CB0.description: Explains what motivates a person’s choices (e.g. a young person gets up early to train because he/she wants to do well in a sport; a group organizes a neighbourhood composting system because it believes that small actions will ensure the future of the planet)

E70BB0A6718442119D34449F3956B3C2.description: Gives the motives behind individual or group choices in the exercise of freedom (e.g. desires, needs, convictions, values, age, education, norms and physical or social constraints)

DED00A3F339E4ACDA53C41ADEF1C283A.description: Describes different types of freedom (e.g. freedom to act [ability to act as one wishes]; freedom of expression [ability to express oneself without fear of reprisal]; freedom of association [ability to join others with a shared objective])

4AE4B40BA0CF46038CFF7D2B32516595.description: Gives different definitions of freedom (e.g. situation of a person who is not dependent on anyone or anything; ability to act without constraints)

056EA41FAC524734BC8C7EB0D72B1B08.description: Knowledge related to ethics themes: Competency 1 - Reflects on ethical questions
